Pelagic cormorants (Phalacrocorax pelagicus) initiate breeding when females produce a clutch of approximately 3.7 eggs [N_R_i = a clutch of approximately 3.7 eggs] per nesting attempt, and field observations indicate that most pairs raise a single brood each year [F_R_i = a single brood each year] under the thermal conditions characteristic of their active metabolic period at 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. Newly hatched chicks emerge at a remarkably modest wet weight of approximately 35 grams [Wwb = approximately 35 grams], a value that reflects the semi-precocial developmental mode typical of cormorants. The initial egg mass, representing the wet weight of the freshly laid egg, has been recorded at 42 grams [Ww0 = 42 grams], indicating substantial maternal investment in yolk and albumen prior to incubation. Incubation itself proceeds at a regulated temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], and under these conditions the embryonated egg develops for an average of 26.5 days [ab = an average of 26.5 days] before pipping and hatching occur. This incubation period is consistent with values reported for other medium-sized Phalacrocorax species and is closely tied to the thermal stability provided by the brood patch of the attending adult.

Following hatching, the altricial nestling enters a phase of rapid somatic growth fueled by intensive biparental provisioning. Under the thermal regime of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and nest departure, occurs at 45 days after hatching [tx = 45 days after hatching]. This developmental timeline places the Pelagic cormorant at the intermediate end of the fledging-age spectrum among congeners, reflecting the energetic demands of growing functional flight feathers and attaining sufficient body condition for independent locomotion. Sexual maturation, marked by the full development of gonadal tissue and the onset of gametogenesis, is reached considerably later than fledging, with puberty estimated at 135 days after hatching [tp = 135 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. This delay between fledging and reproductive maturity is a common life-history pattern among seabirds, allowing juveniles to refine foraging skills and accumulate sufficient body reserves before undertaking the high costs of reproduction.

Adult body mass exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in this species, a trait that influences foraging ecology and reproductive energetics. Females attain an ultimate wet weight of 1702 grams [Wwi = 1702 grams], whereas males reach a substantially greater ultimate wet weight of 2041 grams [Wwi = 2041 grams], a difference of nearly 20% that likely reflects divergent selective pressures related to territory defense and courtship display. These asymptotic masses are achieved gradually over the subadult years as individuals refine their diving proficiency and expand their dietary breadth along coastal rocky shorelines. The maximum lifespan documented for this species, under natural conditions and the thermal regime of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C] associated with active metabolism, is approximately 17.8 years [am = approximately 17.8 years], a longevity that is comparable to that of other small-to-medium-sized cormorants and aligns with a relatively slow life-history strategy characterized by delayed maturity and extended reproductive windows. Senescent individuals typically exhibit a gradual decline in foraging efficiency and reproductive output before natural death occurs.

First successful reproduction in Pelagic cormorants is not attempted immediately upon reaching sexual maturity; instead, individuals typically defer their first breeding effort until approximately 1.4 years after hatching [tR = approximately 1.4 years after hatching], when they are operating at 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. This delay between puberty and first brood production is a well-documented phenomenon in colonial seabirds, attributed to the need for young birds to secure a stable nesting territory, acquire a compatible mate, and accumulate sufficient lipid reserves to sustain the extended incubation and chick-rearing periods. During this pre-breeding interval, subadult birds may engage in prospecting behaviors, visiting potential colony sites and observing experienced breeders without themselves attempting to nest. The annual reproductive output that follows remains modest, constrained by the single-brood breeding strategy typical of high-latitude cormorants, with each successful pair producing a single clutch per annual reproductive season [F_R_i = a single clutch per annual reproductive season], containing approximately 3.7 eggs [N_R_i = containing approximately 3.7 eggs]. This conservative reproductive rate is balanced by relatively high adult survival and extended lifespan.

Comparative life-history analyses across the Phalacrocoracidae reveal that the Pelagic cormorant occupies an intermediate position along the slow-fast continuum, with its age at first reproduction of 1.4 years after hatching [tR = 1.4 years after hatching] being slightly earlier than that of larger congeners such as the Great cormorant at a temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. The hatchling wet weight of 35 grams [Wwb = 35 grams] represents approximately 2% of the ultimate female adult mass of 1702 grams [Wwi = 1702 grams], a ratio that is typical for altricial seabird species and underscores the extensive postnatal parental investment required. Under the active metabolic temperature regime of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], the fledging period of 45 days after hatching [tx = 45 days after hatching] and the pubertal milestone of 135 days after hatching [tp = 135 days after hatching] are closely linked to the seasonal availability of schooling fish prey along the North Pacific coast. These demographic parameters, collected from long-term colony monitoring studies, provide the empirical foundation for population viability models and inform conservation strategies for this climate-sensitive seabird across its breeding range.
